1.note: Rimmon-perez is a station of the Israelites in the wilderness (Num 33:19). The name is chosen for the rhyme with בַּפָּרֶץ ("in the breach") in the next line; it is not a real town of the author's time.

2.note: 2 Sam 11:1 "at the time when kings go out", that is, spring. Here the "kings" may also be the lights of heaven that come out in the spring sky.

3.note: The rhyme words of these lines are פֶּחָם (their governor, from פֶּחָה), פֶּחָם (coal), חָם (Ham) and נִצְחָם: the same sound in different senses.

4.note: That is, the day is himself a slave to toil (as the next lines say), sold with no right of redemption. The phrase has no clear biblical source.

5.note: Job 38:19 "where is the way where light dwells". The night argues that the dark pupil, not the white of the eye, is where sight (light) lives.

6.note: Job 7:4 "I am full of tossings until the dawn", of sleepless nights. The night turns the verse: it is the day that fills lovers with wandering (נְדוּדִים also means being driven apart). The rhyme דוֹדִים / נְדוּדִים (love / wanderings) is lost.

7.he: וְעָלְתָה עָשׁ וְרִמָּה. עַל עָשׁ וְכִימָה
7.note: A pun: the first עָשׁ is the moth, with the worm the image of what is lowly (Job 25:6, Isa 51:8); the second עָשׁ is a constellation (Job 9:9, usually the Bear). The low (the night) has risen over the high (the day).

8.note: Job 22:5 "is not your evil great". Unpointed, רעותיך can also be read "your female companions", which fits the next line about females sent to war.

9.note: "Your shame" is the sun, mocked as a shameful thing (בֹּשֶׁת is a biblical name for an idol, Jer 11:13). The next line pairs it with גְּבִרְתֶּךָ, "your lady".

10.note: סַפַּחַת is a skin eruption in the laws of leprosy (Lev 13:2). The day answers in kind below, calling the moon a בַּהֶרֶת, a bright spot from the same verse. "Flees" is literal; the sense may be a mark that fades away.

11.note: Lev 13:4 "a white bright spot", a sign of leprosy. לְבָנָה (white) is also a word for the moon, so the phrase can be heard as "like the spot that is the moon".

12.note: נְסוּכָה is read as "anointed, installed", from Ps 2:6 "I have set (נָסַכְתִּי) my king".

13.note: A pun on the hero's name: חֶבֶר (Ḥever) and חָבֵר (companion) have the same letters. Compare Ps 119:63 "I am a companion to all who fear You".
